why: Concrete, student acts on their own map; B's 'wanting and should' is pictureable and shorter in framing than a four-risk list.
Keeps the author's first-person scar story and voice, which the taste rules protect.
Guess prompt comes before the reveal in a way that tells them to watch the second session, and the answer isn't spoiled before the guess.
Student shapes the rules together with the agent rather than just receiving a draft.
Shorter; B's added line is a vague 'possible problem' that adds little.
'Session' is the concept word students actually work in; 'run' is vaguer.
Title states the point and the picturable idea; the added closing line in B is redundant with it, and 'The generalisation' is abstract.
Ties back to what the student actually ran (M6 encode loop) and closes with a memorable flywheel line.
Shorter; the added clause in B is filler.
Puts the student in control: the kit they grow themselves is the one that counts.
'Exercise' names what students recognise; 'prompts' is less accurate for the comparison.
Cleaner, shorter phrasing of the same point.
Shorter and concrete; B's forward reference to Module 4 is an abstraction the student can't picture yet.
Shorter, and 'YOUR real work is the material' keeps the emphasis without the stiffer phrasing.
'The move is the same every time' tells the student there is a repeatable pattern they can use.
Shorter, and the added phase preview in B is orientation the student doesn't need on this slide.
Shorter, and the removed sentence only restated the loop.
'It often isn't. It's a draft…' is a clean, direct phrasing and matches the other slide's wording.
Drops the 'you are not learning them here' line, which tells the student to wait and adds words.
Keeps the student acting ('Ask these one at a time'). B has them watch instead of type.
'Three' is a count the reader would have to verify, and A reads the same without it.
The title no longer commits to a count and is shorter.
'Three agents using the file' is a concrete picture, where 'Where the file gets read' is vaguer.
Shorter and has the student looking at what the tool list leaves out, which is a concrete thing to check.
Adds a short line that puts the practice in the student's hands and ties the modules together.
Shorter and punchier, and the first-person 'I pushed back' line carries the author's voice.
'This is your side-quest lane' orients the student at a window switch.
Shorter, and the added opener is redundant hedging.
'Read what Claude proposes' is the more concrete verb; 'Check' is vaguer.
'Forest before the trees' is a concrete image the student can picture, and the line is shorter.
The title states the whole idea, with the problem and its fix, in plain words.
The title tells the student what to do, which puts them in control; B only describes a quirk.
Shorter and gives a concrete command, `/statusline`.
'ADR' is the clearer, more concrete term; B's replacement is vaguer.
Names 'The wall' as a concept the student can use, and keeps the author's voice.
The title makes a concrete, memorable claim instead of a generic abstraction.
Shorter title; 'window' still carries the concept.
The added line is a generic caveat that dilutes the author's first-person point; shorter wins.
The title no longer fixes the count, and it reads shorter.
The student sees the concrete action: ask Claude to spot generic pages and propose a sharpening for each. B's imperative is vaguer.
A keeps the closing line that frames the phases as places rather than a pipeline. B drops it.
A keeps the permission line 'You don't need to get it right first time'.
A is concrete and puts the student in action: plan mode, push back in your own words. B is abstract and warns about over-consuming.
B adds orientation before the lectures and says why each one is there.
B adds 'gives you the floor', which puts the student in control, and 'swap a file path' is concrete. 'Committed change' is a bit odd, but B wins overall.
